items.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007
items.q: You and I spoke the next thing we know we have “Havin’ a Good Time” with Joe Williams.

ctx.x: Yeah, that’s not what I mean.

Yeah. No. I got a stash of tapes that no one’s ever heard. I have a way that I do compilations. I have this little area, I started playing it because when I came back after that slump in the early eighties I had to come up with something new. Because the pop records I was making and the jazz records I was making, nobody really wanted. So, this © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

is too long a story to bore you with but through a friend, Bernie Dreighton, I found some tapes he had made at a small club in Brooklyn in the sixties: Blakey, Kenny Dorham, you know, people like that, guys who’d play these small clubs in Brooklyn to work out material before they recorded for Blue Note or Prestige or stuff like that. So in trying to clear those, I came across other collections. At a certain point we had isolated a quarter of a million hours of privately — in lieu of the word illegally — recorded…

items.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007
items.q: I play Joe Williams records ‘cause I love Joe Williams... he knew it, and we were his guy in that town.

ctx.x: Well it’s really interesting too on the Joe Williams CD. You hear him talking to the audience and all that, and that’s great.

But that’s what — when you went to a club, you know, like for instance I saw Joe fifty times in Philly. Because he always played Philly once a year, he played Showboat or Pep’s. And he was a charming entertainer. And he kidded around with the audience and he knew people in each city. Let me tell you how smart Joe was. Whenever I would walk into the club, I usually caught the last set ‘cause I got off the air at one and the last set © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

was at one twenty. And you know, on the weekends if it was crowded, he knew how to work disc jockeys, so he always came up — nobody said “Joe Williams,” the trio played, he walked out, he would go into a song and then he would say “good evening I’m Joseph Goreed Williams.” He had this thing, I’m Joe Williams, I’m from Chicago, I’m here to entertain you.
